list-item.p: Deferasirox reduced the hazard of progression/death (HR 0.41–0.44, P < .05) and TRM (HR 0.21, P = .035) in AML and MDS.
Results are robust to unmeasured confounding (E-values >3.5) across propensity score-matched models.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Iron overload after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) is associated with oxidative stress and adverse outcomes. Although deferasirox reduces ferritin, its effect on survival remains incompletely characterized. We conducted a prospective observational study across 7 French centers, enrolling 41 patients with acute myeloid leukemia or myelodysplastic syndromes who initiated deferasirox 6 months after allo-HSCT. Eligibility required complete remission, iron overload (ferritin level >1000 μg/L), and preserved organ function. Outcomes were compared with propensity score–matched controls (1:2) from the SFGM-TC registry. End points were overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), transplant-related mortality (TRM), relapse, and safety. Analyses employed exact matching, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and multivariable Cox models. Ferritin level decreased from 1700 μg/L to <1000 μg/L by 18 months. Across analytic methods, deferasirox was associated with a reduced hazard of progression or death (PFS: hazard ratio [HR], 0.41-0.44) and a reduced hazard of mortality (OS: HR, 0.28-0.43). TRM was significantly reduced in propensity score matching and Cox models (HR, 0.21), whereas the IPTW analysis yielded a comparable point estimate (HR, 0.24) that did not reach the significance threshold (P = .063). The probability of relapse (estimated via cumulative incidence of relapse) did not differ significantly. Adverse events were predominantly renal and manageable. Initiating deferasirox 6 months after allo-HSCT was associated with sustained ferritin reduction, a reduced hazard of progression or death (PFS), lower TRM, and a favorable although nonsignificant hazard of mortality (OS), with acceptable safety. These findings support deferasirox as a feasible posttransplant intervention, warranting confirmation in randomized trials.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Iron overload (IO) has emerged as a significant driver of morbidity and mortality in patients with hematologic malignancies undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT).1, 2, 3, 4, 5 Repeated erythrocyte transfusions result in excess iron accumulation (primarily non–transferrin-bound ferrous iron) that catalyzes the Fenton reaction and generates deleterious hydroxyl radicals. These radicals inflict rapid damage on DNA, proteins, and lipids, initiating oxidative stress that undermines mitochondrial integrity (eg, loss of membrane potential and mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening) and activates cell-death pathways, including apoptosis and ferroptosis, contributing to organ injury and dysfunction.6,7 Beyond its direct cytotoxic effects, iron chelation shows mechanistic promise in promoting leukemic blast differentiation via the induction of reactive oxygen species and activation of the MAPK/JNK pathway.8 Although hyperferritinemia is a nonspecific biomarker, elevated in contexts such as inflammation, infection, hepatic dysfunction, or active malignancies, it is an accessible surrogate strongly correlated with IO.5 Elevated pretransplant ferritin level consistently correlates with adverse outcomes, including diminished overall survival (OS) and heightened transplant-related mortality (TRM).9, 10, 11 Emerging data also implicate hyperferritinemia after transplantation in compromised survival, justifying the use of iron chelation therapy after allo-HSCT.10 In a multicenter trial,11 deferasirox administered ∼168 days posttransplant significantly reduced serum ferritin levels and achieved negative iron stores in 84% of participants, with an acceptable safety profile. Retrospective analyses12 further indicate that posttransplant deferasirox use after transplantation may enhance OS and progression-free survival (PFS), and in one study, association with reduced cumulative relapse rates, potentially mediated by higher incidence of chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD).10 Despite these insights, no standardized guidelines exist to manage IO in allo-HSCT recipients, although most long-term follow-up protocols advocate monitoring iron levels for at least 1 year.6 Crucially, to date, no randomized controlled trials or prospective quasi-experimental studies (designed to mitigate selection bias) have evaluated the effects of deferasirox on OS or PFS 6 months after allo-HSCT in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) or myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS). To address this gap, we conducted a prospective observational study across 7 French centers, registered within the SFGM-TC registry. Deferasirox was administered from 6 months after allo-HSCT to minimize early toxicity. Outcomes were compared with propensity score–matched control patients who did not receive iron chelation, drawn from the same registry. The primary objective was to assess the impact of deferasirox on OS and PFS beginning at 6 months after allo-HSCT in patients with AML/MDS.

sec.title: Patients and methods
sec.p: This was a prospective, nonrandomized observational study in which treated patients meeting predefined eligibility criteria were offered deferasirox at 6 months posttransplant as part of standard clinical care, with prospective data collection. In accordance with the French Public Health Code in force at the time the study was initiated, this study was classified as noninterventional because all procedures were conducted in the usual course of care without any additional diagnostic, therapeutic, or monitoring interventions beyond standard practice. As such, the study did not involve any modification of patient management and did not introduce any risk or constraint for participants. Given its strictly observational nature and the absence of intervention, this study was approved by the French Advisory Committee on Health Research Information processing and the French Data Protection Authority before initiation. The study was conducted in accordance with French regulatory requirements and the Declaration of Helsinki. The nonrandomized design introduces potential selection bias, which we addressed through propensity score methods (exact matching and inverse probability of treatment weighting [IPTW]) and multiple sensitivity analyses.

The primary objective was to evaluate the effect of deferasirox on OS and PFS and the secondary objectives were to evaluate the effect of deferasirox on TRM to estimate the probability of relapse and to evaluate deferasirox toxicity.

sec.title: Study patients
sec.p: This prospective observational study involved patients treated with the oral iron chelator deferasirox (hereafter referred to as treated) and compared their outcomes to matched retrospective patients who did not receive the treatment (hereafter referred to as controls), using the data of patients who underwent allo-HSCT and were registered in the SFGM-TC registry.

Both treated and control groups met the following inclusion criteria: diagnosis of AML or MDS, age ≥18 years at diagnosis, achievement of complete remission (CR) within 6 months after allo-HSCT, undergoing allo-HSCT from 2014 onward, intermediate II or adverse/high-risk score using European LeukemiaNet (ELN) 2010 classification (AML) or International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS; MDS), receiving treatment at 1 of 7 participating French allo-HSCT centers (CH Lyon Sud, IUCT Oncopole, Toulouse; CHU Bordeaux; CHU Montpellier; CHU Saint-Étienne; CHU Nancy; or Hôpital Saint-Louis, Paris), and availability of allo-HSCT data in the SFGM-TC ProMISe registry. T patients also had to meet the following criteria at the baseline visit (6 months after allo-HSCT): evidence of IO defined by serum ferritin level >1000 μg/L; preserved renal function with serum creatinine level <1.5 × upper limit of normal (ULN) and estimated creatinine clearance >60 mL/min; proteinuria <1 g per 24 hours; preserved liver function with alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase levels <2× ULN and total bilirubin level <2× ULN; no concomitant use of another iron chelator; no active viral infections (hepatitis B or C or HIV); no prolonged QT interval on electrocardiogram; no history of ocular toxicity related to iron chelation; not pregnant or breastfeeding; no history of alcohol addiction; and provision of written informed consent.

sec.title: Evaluation and treatment
sec.p: Treatment response in AML was defined according to the 2010 ELN13 recommendations. CR required bone marrow blasts <5%, absence of circulating or extramedullary disease, absolute neutrophil count ≥ 1.0 × 109/L, platelet count ≥ 100 × 109/L, and independence from red-cell transfusion; CR with incomplete hematologic recovery met these same criteria except for persistent neutropenia or thrombocytopenia. Relapse was defined as the recurrence of leukemic disease following CR or CR with incomplete hematologic recovery, manifesting either as leukemic blasts in peripheral blood, >5% blasts in bone marrow unexplained by treatment effects, cytologically confirmed extramedullary disease, or the reappearance of the patient’s original cytogenetic or molecular abnormality.

For MDS, response criteria followed the 2006 International Working Group definitions14: CR required a normocellular marrow with ≤5% myeloblasts, no circulating blasts, and recovery of peripheral blood counts (hemoglobin level ≥ 11 g/dL, platelet count ≥ 100 × 109/L, and absolute neutrophil count ≥ 1.0 × 109/L) each sustained over at least 2 weekly assessments. Partial remission was defined by a ≥50% reduction in bone marrow blasts from pretreatment levels whereas remaining above 5%. Relapse was evidenced by a return to pretreatment blast levels, a ≥50% decline from peak remission levels in granulocytes or platelets, or a ≥1.5 g/dL drop in hemoglobin level or renewed transfusion dependence.

sec.title: Iron chelation
sec.p: For the treatment group, the baseline assessment occurred at 6 months after allo-HSCT, which also marked the initiation of deferasirox. Subsequent follow-up evaluations were conducted at 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 months relative to this baseline. Deferasirox (Exjade) was commenced at a low initial dose to mitigate toxicity: either 7 mg/kg per day using film-coated tablets or 10 mg/kg per day using dispersible tablets, administered according to the specifications of the respective formulation.15

In addition to standard allo-HSCT medical follow-up, serum ferritin levels were measured at each visit, and clinical tolerance to deferasirox was assessed to guide treatment decisions, whether to continue therapy, adjust the dose, or temporarily or permanently discontinue treatment. Permanent discontinuation was left to the investigator’s discretion once serum ferritin dropped below 1000 μg/L, based on measurements obtained during a scheduled study visit.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Analyses were performed using R (version 4.3.0), with the tidyverse, survminer, cobalt, WeightIt, and Match packages.

Descriptive statistics were reported as medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs) for continuous variables that deviated from normality, and as means with standard deviations for normally distributed data. Categorical variables were presented as counts and percentages.

Comparative analyses employed the χ2 test or Fisher exact test for categorical variables, and, contingent on distribution, the Student t test, F test, or Wilcoxon rank-sum test for comparisons of continuous outcomes. Statistical significance was determined using a 2-sided α-level of 0.05. No correction for multiple testing was applied.

Survival analyses were conducted using left truncation at 6 months post–allo-HSCT, coinciding with the initiation of deferasirox, to mitigate immortal time bias. OS was defined from this time until death from any cause, with censoring at the date last known alive. PFS was assessed among patients in CR, measured from 6 months post–allo-HSCT until relapse or death, with censoring at last follow-up. The cumulative incidence of relapse was estimated among patients in CR, with relapse as the event of interest and death in remission treated as a competing risk. TRM was defined as death not attributable to the underlying disease; patients experiencing relapse were censored at relapse as survivors. The probability of relapse was estimated among patients in CR using cumulative incidence functions to account for death in remission as a competing risk. Survival distributions for OS and PFS were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method. Survival distributions were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and compared using the log-rank test.16,17 Follow-up data were obtained from the ProMISe registry (see “Data collection” and Figure 1 for details).Figure 1.
Flowchart of the study. The flowchart shows the selection process for the 41 deferasirox-treated patients (left panel) and 82 propensity score–matched controls from the SFGM-TC ProMISe registry (right panel). The infused population (n = 991) was analyzed using 3 complementary approaches: exact 1:2 PSM, IPTW, and multivariable Cox regression with cGVHD adjustment. ∗Exclusion criteria included age <18 years, relapse or death before 6 months after allo-HSCT, >2 allo-HSCT history, and unfavorable prognostic scores (ELN 2010 for AML and IPSS for MDS).

To address potential selection bias, propensity score matching (PSM)18 was used to balance baseline covariates between prospectively enrolled patients treated with deferasirox and retrospective controls from the ProMISe registry. Propensity scores were estimated via multivariable logistic regression, incorporating age, sex, disease subtype (AML vs MDS), prognostic score (ELN 2010 for AML; IPSS14 for MDS), allo-HSCT sequence (first vs second), transplant center, donor type, stem cell source, conditioning regimen, and acute GVHD (aGVHD) grade. aGVHD was not modeled as a time-dependent covariate because it typically occurred within 100 days after allo-HSCT (ie, before deferasirox initiation).19,20

Two approaches were applied to estimate the average treatment effect on the treated: (1) exact matching without replacement, pairing each treated patient with 2 controls (1:2) within a caliper width of 0.15 on the logit of the propensity score, with exact matching enforced for ELN score, sex, and disease subtype21 and (2) IPTW, weighting treated patients by the inverse of their propensity score and controls by the inverse of 1 minus the score. Balance was evaluated by absolute standardized mean differences and proportion differences, visualized with love plots and density distributions of propensity scores and covariates before and after matching. OS, PFS, and TRM were analyzed using time-dependent Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for cGVHD and applied to the matched data set. Sensitivity analyses assessed robustness to unmeasured confounding using the E-value,22 which quantifies the minimum strength of association an unmeasured confounder would require with both treatment and outcome to fully explain the observed association. In addition, an unmatched time-dependent Cox model adjusting for the full set of covariates was used to evaluate consistency across analytic strategies and to assess potential bias introduced by PSM-related exclusions.

We employed 3 complementary analytic strategies to enhance robustness: PSM provides matched comparisons, IPTW retains full sample size and balances covariates, and Cox regression directly adjusts for confounders. Convergent findings across methods with different assumptions strengthen causal inference.23,24

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: Two data sets were analyzed in this study. The first comprised exclusively the treated patients and included deferasirox-related variables, namely treatment characteristics, adverse events (AE), and iron metabolism parameters. The second data set encompassed both treated and control cohorts, derived from the ProMISe registry, and comprised diagnostic data, allo-HSCT details, such as the occurrence of aGVHD and cGVHD, as well as long-term follow-up data beyond the 24-month visit.

All patients had complete follow-up through the SFGM-TC ProMISe registry, which systematically captures long-term outcomes for allo-HSCT recipients. Vital status and disease progression were updated through routine clinical evaluations and registry reporting procedures.
The maximum follow-up duration from the ProMISe registry was 107 months after baseline.

sec.title: General characteristics of treated patients who received iron
sec.p:
A total of 41 patients (Figure 1) were enrolled between March 2016 and February 2022 across 7 allo-HSCT centers and initiated deferasirox at baseline (ie, 6 months after allo-HSCT). The population was predominantly male (27/41 [66%]; Table 1). The median age at diagnosis was 58 years (range, 20-70 years). Most patients had AML (35/41 [85%]), and 6 patients among 41 (15%) had MDS. Within the AML subgroup, the most common World Health Organization subtype was AML with maturation (7/35 [20%]), whereas among the MDS cases, refractory anemia with excess blasts-2 predominated (4/6 [67%]).Table 1.

Before transplantation, Sorror comorbidity indices ranged from 1 to 5 (5/14 [36%] had a score of 1). According to ELN 2010 and IPSS risk classifications, 31 of 41 (76%) of patients were categorized as intermediate II and 10 of 41 (24%) as adverse/high risk (10/41). Cytogenetic analysis revealed a normal karyotype in 19 of 41 (46%) and an abnormal karyotype in 22 of 41 (54%). The distribution of recurrent gene mutations was provided in the supplemental Figure 1.

The median time from diagnosis to HSCT was 7 months (range, 1-81 months). Most patients underwent their first allo-HSCT (39/41 [95%]), whereas 2 received a second transplant. Concerning donor type, 29% of the patients were HLA-identical siblings, 17% mismatched (related or unrelated), and 54% unrelated matched. Peripheral blood was the predominant HSC source (90%), and myeloablative conditioning was administered in 27% of cases.
Median ferritin levels were elevated before HSCT (1529 μg/L; range, 14-4157) and slightly higher at the initiation of deferasirox (1697 μg/L; range, 1000-10 041).

During follow-up, serum ferritin levels declined progressively after the initiation of deferasirox (Figure 2). Median ferritin levels decreased from 1700 μg/L at baseline (month 0) to <1000 μg/L by month 18, with a persistent decrease until month 24. Variability in ferritin level was greatest at baseline and early time points, as reflected by wider IQRs and several high outliers (>5000-10 000 μg/L). In contrast, later assessments demonstrated both lower medians and reduced dispersion, consistent with sustained iron chelation.Figure 2.
Ferritinemia evolution after allo-HSCT in deferasirox-treated patients (N = 41). Box plots show serum ferritin levels (μg/L) before allo-HSCT, at baseline (month 0 and 6 months after allo-HSCT when deferasirox was initiated), and at 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 months after treatment initiation. The horizontal black line indicates the 1000 μg/L IO threshold. The boxes represent IQRs with median values. Median ferritin level decreased from 1697 μg/L at baseline to <1000 μg/L by month 18.

Regarding GVHD, 48% of patients remained free of aGVHD, 33% developed a grade 1, and 20% developed a grade 2, whereas cGVHD occurred in 32% of patients. Two patients died at 15.8 and 17.1 months after baseline, whereas 39 remained alive at the last follow-up of the prospective study (treated group). Relapse occurred in 15% of patients (6/41), and 4 additional deaths were recorded (4/39). In total, 6 deaths were observed, 2 (33%) were related to HSCT and 4 (67%) were from the progression of the underlying disease.

sec.title: PSM and IPTW procedures
sec.p:
For PSM, a subset of 1861 patients with AML/MDS in the ProMISe database who had undergone allo-HSCT and had not received iron chelation therapy was analyzed. Of these, 950 patients were eligible for PSM (Figure 1). An “infused” pool of 991 patients was generated by combining the 41 treated patients with the 950 untreated controls. Using exact matching with a 1:2 (treated-to-control) ratio, the PSM procedure yielded a matched cohort comprising 82 controls whose baseline covariates were well balanced relative to the treated group (Table 2). After matching, absolute standardized mean differences for all covariates were <0.10, confirming adequate balance (supplemental Figure 2). Balance plots demonstrated substantial covariate overlap between groups, supporting the robustness of the matching process. Similarly, after IPTW, all standardized mean differences remained <0.10, indicating adequate covariate balance, and balance plots were also consistent (supplemental Figure 3).Table 2.

sec.title: Survival analysis
sec.p:
In the propensity score–matched (1:2) cohort without adjustment for cGVHD, median OS and PFS were not reached in either group. OS did not differ significantly between the treated and control groups (Figure 3A), with a P value resting just above the threshold for significance (P = .057). Long-term survival remained higher in patients receiving chelation therapy: 5-year OS was 0.81 (95% CI, 0.69-0.96) in the treated deferasirox patients vs 0.72 (95% CI, 0.62-0.84) in the control patients. PFS was significantly improved in the treated group (P = .034; Figure 3B), with 5-year PFS of 0.78 (95% CI, 0.66-0.93) for the treated group vs 0.59 (95% CI, 0.47-0.73) for the control group. TRM was also significantly lower with chelation (P = .02; Figure 3C), with a cumulative incidence of TRM at 5 years of 6.1% (95% CI, 0.0-14.1) and 20.9% (95% CI, 10.5-30.1) for the treated and control groups, respectively, whereas the probability of relapse did not differ significantly (estimated via competing risk analysis) (P = .49). The 5-year probability estimates were 16.1% (95% CI, 3.4-27.2) and 25% (95% CI, 10.8-36.9) at 5 years for the treated and control groups, respectively.Figure 3.
Survival according to deferasirox status, after PSM with exact (1:2) matching and without cGVHD adjustment. Kaplan–Meier curves and cumulative incidence curves for the matched cohort (41 treated and 82 controls) with left truncation at 6 months post–allo-HSCT. (A) OS: 5-year OS, 0.81 vs 0.72; P = .057; (B) PFS: 5-year PFS, 0.78 vs 0.59; P = .034; (C) Cumulative incidence of TRM: 5-year TRM, 6.1% vs 20.9%; P = .02; (D) Cumulative incidence of relapse (CIR): 5-year CIR, 16.1% vs 25%; P = .49. The blue curves represent deferasirox-treated patients; orange curves, controls.

From the 6-month landmark, median follow-up was 42 months (IQR, 30-54) for the treated group and 36 months (IQR, 18-60) for the control group. Numbers at risk declined over time as expected in transplant cohort studies. In the PSM cohort at 24 months from the 6-month landmark, 34 treated and 50 control patients remained in the risk set for the OS and TRM analyses, with 30 and 43 patients remaining for the PFS analysis, respectively. At 36 months, these numbers were 27 treated vs 39 controls for OS and TRM, and 23 vs 35 for PFS. These retention rates (66%-83% at 24 months and 48%-66% at 36 months) demonstrate adequate follow-up duration for primary end point assessment.

When adjusted for cGVHD, deferasirox exposure was consistently associated with improved outcomes across all analytic approaches (PSM, IPTW, and multivariable Cox model; Table 3). For OS, hazard ratios (HRs) were in favor of the treated group on PSM (HR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.18-1.05; P = .065), IPTW (HR, 0.28; 95% CI, 0.10-0.77; P = .013; E-value, 4.18; 95% CI, 2.5-5.9), and Cox analysis (HR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.15-0.79; P = .003; E-value, 3.52; 95% CI, 1.9-5.2). PFS showed similar benefit on PSM (HR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.20-0.96; P = .039; E-value, 2.9; 95% CI, 1.7-4.1), IPTW (HR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.18-1.02; P = .056), and Cox analysis (HR, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.20-0.84; P = .005; E-value, 3.1; 95% CI, 1.6-4.6). TRM was significantly reduced for the treated group on both PSM (HR, 0.21; 95% CI, 0.05-0.90; P = .035; E-value, 5.17; 95% CI, 3.8-6.5) and Cox analysis (HR, 0.21; 95% CI, 0.05-0.87; P = .006; E-value, 5.17; 95% CI, 3.7-6.7) and had a similar point estimate in the IPTW model (HR, 0.24; 95% CI, 0.05-1.08; P = .063).Table 3.

sec.title: AE related to deferasirox
sec.p: The AE associated with deferasirox therapy were acceptable: acute renal failure (16.7%), diarrhea (7.1%), hepatic cytolysis (4.8%), nausea (4.8%), hepatic cholestasis (2.4%), hematuria (2.4%), headache (2.4%), and asthenia (2.4%). They were reported predominantly 3 months after baseline and decreased gradually until the end of the treatment. Among the patients who experienced gastrointestinal AE attributable to deferasirox, none had chronic gut GVHD at the time of AE occurrence. The median duration of iron chelation was 12.5 months (range, 0.8-24.3). A reduction in dosage occurred in 9.5% of cases. Discontinuation due to an AE, followed by reintroduction, was observed in 12% of cases, and permanent discontinuation was observed in 33% of patients. The main reasons for permanent discontinuation were related to acute renal failure (n = 4) and alteration of renal biomarkers (n = 4).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this prospective observational study of 41 patients with AML/MDS who initiated deferasirox 6 months after allo-HSCT, we observed consistent associations between iron chelation and reduced hazards of disease progression and TRM. Specifically, deferasirox was associated with reduced hazards of progression (HR, 0.41-0.44 across methods) and a reduced hazard of mortality (OS: HR, 0.28-0.43), although findings were not uniformly significant across all models. For TRM, results were significant in 2 of 3 models (PSM and Cox regression), with all estimates directionally favorable. These findings suggest a potential beneficial effect of deferasirox on posttransplant outcomes.

These findings corroborated and extended prior reports by clarifying the timing, magnitude, and safety of iron chelation after transplantation. Importantly, the observed benefit persisted across multiple analytic strategies and remained after adjustment for cGVHD, supporting the robustness of our conclusions.

Our results were consistent with earlier retrospective and smaller prospective series showing that deferasirox reduced ferritin levels, lowered relapse risk, and may have prolonged OS or reduced the hazard of death after allo-HSCT in AML/MDS. For example, Cho et al12 and Sivgin et al25 have documented favorable survival with deferasirox in similar AML populations after allo-HSCT, and meta-analyses in MDS confirmed the adverse prognostic impact of elevated ferritin level as well as the potential benefit of iron chelation on OS. Biologically, these data reinforced the plausibility that IO contributed to oxidative stress, organ damage, and infectious risk, all of which may be ameliorated by chelation.

Of particular note in our study was the significant reduction in TRM with deferasirox in one model, a clinically meaningful end point that reflects nonrelapse mortality and was less likely to be driven by disease biology. Furthermore, our safety data were reassuring: renal events were the most frequently observed toxicity but generally manageable with dose adjustments or discontinuation; this suggested that initiating deferasirox at 6 months posttransplant was feasible with acceptable risk, provided renal function was carefully monitored.

The Sorror score could only be formally calculated for 14 of 41 treated patients due to incomplete granular data required for Sorror scoring in the remaining cases, although major comorbidities were clinically assessed for all patients at inclusion. This prevented comprehensive adjustment for baseline comorbidity burden in our comparative analyses.

The key limitations of our study include the lack of data on phlebotomy use and baseline ferritin levels in control patients. Phlebotomy represents an alternative iron-reduction strategy that was sometimes employed following allo-HSCT at participating centers; its unmeasured use in control patients could have constituted residual confounding in our comparative analyses. In addition, we were unable to assess the association between baseline ferritin levels and treatment outcomes due to the absence of systematic ferritin measurement in control patients from the registry. More broadly, as a nonrandomized study, treatment assignment reflected clinical decision-making and may have been influenced by unmeasured factors affecting prognosis, such as performance status, detailed comorbidity burden, or socioeconomic factors. Although propensity score methods address measured confounding, residual confounding from unmeasured factors cannot be excluded. To quantify the potential impact of such unmeasured confounding, we calculated E-values, which estimated the minimum strength of association that an unmeasured confounder would have needed with both treatment exposure and outcome to fully explain away the observed effect after accounting for measured covariates. In our analyses, the E-values were relatively large (eg, for OS in IPTW: HR, 0.28; E-value ≈ 4.18; TRM in PSM: HR, 0.21; E-value ≈ 5.17), indicating that only a confounder with extremely strong dual associations could have negated the observed benefit of deferasirox. Although unmeasured confounding could not be entirely excluded, the magnitudes of the E-values suggested that its impact was unlikely to be sufficient to overturn our primary findings.26

Methodologically, a strength of our study was the complementary application of multiple causal inference techniques, each with its own strengths and caveats. PSM enhanced internal validity by creating balanced comparison groups, although it excluded unmatched patients and may have reduced generalizability.27 IPTW retained all individuals and emulated a pseudopopulation in which treatment was less confounded by measured covariates, but it may have been sensitive to extreme weights and therefore had larger variance.28 The multivariable Cox model, although more traditional and less constrained by matching or weighting, depended on correct model specification and assumed that measured covariates sufficed to adjust confounding.29 The fact that deferasirox’s benefit appeared in PSM, IPTW, and Cox analyses strengthened confidence that our findings were not merely statistical artifacts.

Nevertheless, limitations remained. Our sample size was modest, particularly for confirming differences in OS, and we relied on ferritin level as a surrogate measure of iron burden, which has known imperfections. More precise biomarkers, such as liver iron concentration assessed by magnetic resonance imaging, labile plasma iron, or non–transferrin-bound iron, should be included in future studies. Although AE were generally tolerable, treatment discontinuation rates were nontrivial, and long-term safety in an allo-HSCT population deserved ongoing monitoring.

In summary, our findings suggested that in patients with AML/MDS who began deferasirox 6 months after allo-HSCT, iron chelation was associated with clinically meaningful improvements in PFS, as well as point estimates favoring deferasirox for OS and TRM, which warrant further investigation in larger cohorts. These observations supported deferasirox as a viable intervention after transplantation, although randomized controlled trials are warranted to confirm our results, compare iron-reduction strategies (eg, chelation vs phlebotomy), and optimize patient selection, treatment timing, and duration to maximize benefit and minimizing risk.
